44300.m: Women in the USA have been able to vote nationwide since 1920.

44301.q: Which amendment ended Prohibition, the ban on alcohol, in 1933?
44301.e: The alcohol ban was based on the 18th Amendment, which was ratified in 1919 and came into force in 1920. The 21st Amendment is so far the only one that repeals an earlier amendment.

44302.q: To what age did the 26th Amendment lower the voting age in the USA in 1971?
44302.e: Before that, the voting age in many states was 21. One argument was that 18-year-olds had to fight in the Vietnam War but were not allowed to vote.
44302.m: Since 1971 you can vote in the USA from the age of 18.

44303.q: Which amendment was proposed in 1789 but only ratified in 1992?
44303.e: The 27th Amendment says that pay rises for members of Congress only take effect after the next election. A student started a campaign for its ratification in the 1980s.
44303.m: The 27th Amendment took more than 200 years to be ratified.

44304.q: How many states must approve an amendment for it to become part of the US Constitution?
44304.e: After being proposed by two thirds of both chambers, Article V requires ratification by three quarters of the states. With 50 states that is 38.
44304.m: An amendment needs the approval of 38 states.

44305.q: Which chamber of the US Congress brings the charges in impeachment proceedings?
44305.e: The House of Representatives passes the articles of impeachment by simple majority. The actual trial then takes place in the Senate.
44305.m: In impeachment, the House of Representatives brings the charges.

44306.q: What majority does the US Senate need to remove an impeached person from office?
44306.e: A conviction requires two thirds of the senators present. This high hurdle has never been reached for a president.
44306.m: To remove someone from office, the Senate needs a two-thirds majority.

44307.q: Who presides over the trial in the Senate when a US President is impeached?
44307.e: The Constitution names the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court as presiding officer. The Vice President would be biased, since he could benefit from the outcome himself.
44307.m: In the impeachment of a president, the Chief Justice presides over the trial.

44308.q: Which US President was the first to be impeached by the House of Representatives, in 1868?
44308.e: After the Civil War, Andrew Johnson clashed with Congress over Reconstruction. In the Senate, just one vote was missing for his removal.
44308.m: In 1868 Andrew Johnson was the first US President to be impeached.

44309.q: Which US President was impeached in 1998 for perjury and obstruction of justice?
44309.e: The impeachment followed the Lewinsky affair. The Senate acquitted Clinton in 1999, and he stayed in office until 2001.
44309.m: Bill Clinton was impeached in 1998 and acquitted in 1999.

44310.q: Which US President is so far the only one to have been impeached twice by the House of Representatives (as of 2025)?
44310.e: The impeachments came in 2019 over the Ukraine affair and in 2021 after the storming of the Capitol. In both Senate trials the necessary majority was not reached.
44310.m: Donald Trump is the only US President impeached twice.

44311.q: Why was there no impeachment trial in the Senate for Richard Nixon in 1974?
44311.e: Because of the Watergate affair, Nixon faced almost certain impeachment and removal. In August 1974 he became the only US President so far to resign.
44311.m: Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 before it came to impeachment.

44312.q: What grounds for impeachment does the US Constitution name?
a: Treason, bribery and other high crimes
44312.e: Article II names “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors”. What exactly falls under this is ultimately decided by Congress.
44312.m: Impeachment requires treason, bribery or serious offences.

44313.q: How many electors does the Electoral College have in total?
44313.e: The number matches the seats of both chambers of Congress together, plus the electors of the capital, Washington, D.C.

44314.q: How is the number of electors of a US state calculated?
a: Members of the House of Representatives plus 2
Only by the area of the state
Number of inhabitants divided by 1 million
44314.e: Each state has as many electors as seats in Congress. That is its members of the House of Representatives plus its Senate seats.
44314.m: A state has as many electors as members of Congress.

44315.q: How many electors does the capital district, Washington, D.C., have?
44315.e: Since the 23rd Amendment of 1961 the capital may take part. It gets as many electors as the smallest state, which is three.

44316.q: Which two states do not award their electors on the “winner takes all” principle (as of 2025)?
44316.e: Maine and Nebraska give two votes to the statewide winner and the rest by congressional district. All other states give all their votes to the winner in the state.
44316.m: Only Maine and Nebraska split their electors.

44317.q: Who elects the US President if nobody gets an absolute majority in the Electoral College?
44317.e: Under the 12th Amendment the House of Representatives then decides, with each state's delegation having only one vote. This last happened in 1825.
44317.m: Without a majority in the Electoral College, the House of Representatives elects the President.

44318.q: Which candidate won more votes nationwide in 2016 but lost in the Electoral College?
44318.e: Hillary Clinton had almost 3 million more votes than Donald Trump. But Trump won more electors because he narrowly won important swing states.
44318.m: In 2016 Hillary Clinton won the popular vote but not the election.

44319.q: Which state has the most electors (2024 and 2028 elections)?
44319.e: After the 2020 census California has 54 electors in total. It is the most populous state in the USA.

44320.q: What is elected in the US midterm elections?
a: The whole House of Representatives and about a third of the Senate
44320.e: The midterms take place halfway through the President's four-year term. All seats in the House of Representatives and about 33 or 34 Senate seats are filled.
44320.m: In the midterms the whole House of Representatives is elected.

44321.q: On which day are US federal elections such as the midterms held?
a: On the Tuesday after the first Monday in November
On the first Sunday in November
On the last Friday in October
44321.e: A law of 1845 fixed election day. It therefore always falls between 2 and 8 November.
44321.m: US elections take place on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

44322.q: Which party usually loses seats in midterm elections?
a: The party with the most senators
44322.e: Historically, the party of the sitting President usually loses seats in the House of Representatives. The election is often seen as a mid-term report on the government.
44322.m: In the midterms the President's party usually loses.

44323.q: Which party won the majority in the House of Representatives in the 2018 midterms?
44323.e: In 2018 the Democrats gained 41 seats and then controlled the House of Representatives. Nancy Pelosi became Speaker again.
44323.m: In 2018 the Democrats won the House of Representatives.

44324.q: What was the result of the 2022 midterm elections in Congress?
a: Republicans won the House, Democrats kept the Senate
Republicans won the Senate, Democrats the House
44324.e: In 2022 the Republicans won a narrow majority in the House of Representatives. The Democrats kept the Senate, so Congress was divided.
44324.m: After the 2022 midterms the US Congress was divided.

44325.q: On which date will the 2026 US midterm elections take place?
44325.e: The first Monday in November 2026 is 2 November. Election day is the Tuesday after that, so 3 November 2026.
44325.m: The 2026 midterms take place on 3 November.

44326.q: How many governorships are up for election in the 2026 midterm elections?
44326.e: Most states elect their governors in midterm years. In 2026, 36 governorships are up for election.
44326.m: In 2026 governors are elected in 36 states.

44327.q: What is a caucus, as opposed to a primary?
a: A party meeting with open discussion
A secret ballot at the polls
44327.e: At a caucus, party members meet in gatherings and often vote openly. In a primary, by contrast, people vote secretly at the polls as in a normal election.
44327.m: A caucus is a party meeting, a primary a ballot at the polls.

44328.q: In which state were the first caucuses of the presidential primaries traditionally held?
44328.e: Since 1972 Iowa traditionally opened the primary season. The Democrats changed their calendar in 2024, but for the Republicans Iowa stayed first.
44328.m: Iowa traditionally opened the primaries with its caucuses.

44329.q: Which state has a law requiring it to hold the country's first primary?
44329.e: A New Hampshire law requires its primary to take place before all similar elections. If necessary, the date is therefore moved earlier.
44329.m: New Hampshire traditionally holds the first primary.

44330.q: What is the day in March called on which particularly many states hold primaries at the same time?
44330.e: On Super Tuesday a large share of the delegates is awarded. Afterwards it is often clear who will win the nomination.
44330.m: On Super Tuesday many states vote at the same time.

a: Only registered party members may vote
Only members of parliament may vote
44331.e: In a closed primary only people registered with the party may vote. In an open primary, independents or members of other parties can also take part.
44331.m: Only party members may take part in a closed primary.

44332.q: Where is a US party's presidential candidate officially nominated after the primaries?
44332.e: The delegates chosen in the primaries meet in summer at the National Convention. There the candidate is formally nominated and the running mate confirmed.
44332.m: The nomination takes place at the national party convention.

44333.q: How many days (excluding Sundays) does the US President have to sign or reject a bill?
44333.e: If the President does nothing within ten days and Congress is in session, the bill becomes law even without a signature.
44333.m: The US President has ten days to decide on a bill.

a: A bill dies because Congress adjourns and the President does not sign
The President strikes out individual budget items
The Supreme Court strikes down a law
44334.e: If Congress adjourns within the ten-day period, the President can simply leave the bill unsigned. This veto cannot be overridden.
44334.m: With a pocket veto the President simply leaves a bill unsigned.

44335.q: Why does the US President not have a line-item veto today?
a: The Supreme Court declared it unconstitutional in 1998
44335.e: The Line Item Veto Act of 1996 allowed individual budget items to be struck out. In Clinton v. City of New York it was struck down in 1998 because it violates the Constitution.
44335.m: Since 1998 the US President has had no line-item veto.

44336.q: Which US President issued the most vetoes, more than 600?
44336.e: In more than twelve years in office, Franklin D. Roosevelt used 635 vetoes. Grover Cleveland comes second.
44336.m: Franklin D. Roosevelt used the veto most often.

44337.q: What does the Latin word “veto” mean?
44337.e: Veto is the first person of “vetare”, to forbid. In ancient Rome the tribunes of the people could already stop decisions with this word.

44338.q: With a regular veto, where does the US President send a bill back to?
a: To the chamber in which it was introduced
44338.e: The President returns the bill with his reasons to the chamber where it started. There Congress can try to override the veto.
44338.m: A rejected bill goes back to the chamber where it began.

44339.q: What is an executive order in the USA?
a: An order from the President to the federal administration
A ruling of the Supreme Court
44339.e: With executive orders the President directs the federal agencies without asking Congress. But they must be based on the Constitution or laws.
44339.m: With executive orders the President gives instructions to the administration.

44340.q: Which organisation did John F. Kennedy found in 1961 by executive order?
44340.e: With Executive Order 10924, Kennedy created the Peace Corps in March 1961. In the same year Congress confirmed it with its own law.
44340.m: The Peace Corps was created in 1961 by an executive order from Kennedy.

44341.q: What did Franklin D. Roosevelt's Executive Order 9066 order in 1942?
a: The internment of people of Japanese descent
The building of the atomic bomb
44341.e: After the attack on Pearl Harbor, about 120,000 people of Japanese origin were taken to camps. In 1988 the US government officially apologised.
44341.m: Executive Order 9066 led to the internment of people of Japanese descent.

44342.q: Which President ended racial segregation in the US armed forces by executive order in 1948?
44342.e: With Executive Order 9981, Truman required equal treatment of all soldiers. Putting it into practice took until the 1950s.
44342.m: In 1948 Truman ended segregation in the military by order.

44343.q: What can happen if an executive order violates the Constitution or a law?
a: It continues to apply unchanged anyway
Only a referendum can stop it
The President can remove the judges
44343.e: In 1952 the Supreme Court ruled that President Truman could not seize steel mills without a legal basis. Executive orders too must be based on the Constitution or laws.
44343.m: Executive orders are also subject to review by the courts.

44344.q: Where are executive orders officially published?
44344.e: The Federal Register is the daily official journal of the US federal government. Executive orders are published there with consecutive numbers.
44344.m: Executive orders appear in the Federal Register.

44345.q: What can a new US President do with his predecessor's executive orders?
a: Revoke them with an order of his own
Change them only with the Senate's approval
44345.e: Because executive orders are not laws, any successor can revoke them. New presidents often cancel many orders on their first day in office.
44345.m: A new President can revoke his predecessor's executive orders.

44346.q: What is the name of the national leadership body of the US Democratic Party?
44346.e: The Democratic National Committee (DNC) was founded in 1848. Among other things it organises the national convention and sets rules for the primaries.
44346.m: The Democratic Party is led nationally by the DNC.

44347.q: In which year was the Democratic Party founded, which today is regarded as the oldest active party in the world?
44347.e: The party emerged in 1828 around Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren. It is regarded as the oldest voter-based party still in existence in the world.
44347.m: The Democratic Party was founded in 1828.

44348.q: What was the name of Democratic President Franklin D. Roosevelt's reform programme during the Great Depression?
44348.e: With the New Deal from 1933, Roosevelt created work programmes, social security and banking rules. He shaped the Democratic Party for decades.
44348.m: Roosevelt fought the economic crisis with the New Deal.

44349.q: Which abbreviation is a well-known nickname for the Republican Party?
44349.e: GOP stands for “Grand Old Party”. The nickname has been in use since the late 19th century.
44349.m: The Republicans are also called the Grand Old Party.

44350.q: In which year was the Republican Party founded, partly to oppose the spread of slavery?
44350.e: Opponents of the spread of slavery into new territories founded the party in 1854. The trigger was the Kansas-Nebraska Act.
44350.m: The Republican Party was founded in 1854.

44351.q: Who was the first Republican President of the USA?
44351.e: Abraham Lincoln won the 1860 election and took office in 1861. He led the Union through the Civil War.
44351.m: Abraham Lincoln was the first Republican President.

44352.q: Which cartoonist made the elephant popular as the symbol of the Republicans in the 19th century?
44352.e: Thomas Nast drew political cartoons for the magazine Harper's Weekly. In an 1874 cartoon he showed Republican voters as an elephant, which has been the party's symbol ever since.
44352.m: Thomas Nast made the elephant the symbol of the Republicans.

44353.q: Which Democratic President was a peanut farmer and Governor of Georgia before his election?
44353.e: Jimmy Carter governed from 1977 to 1981. In 2002 he received the Nobel Peace Prize for his work for peace and human rights.
44353.m: Jimmy Carter was a peanut farmer and Governor of Georgia before becoming President.

44354.q: Which Republican President governed from 1953 to 1961 and was Supreme Allied Commander in Europe in the Second World War?
44354.e: Eisenhower led the Normandy landings in 1944. As President he had the Interstate motorway network built, among other things.
44354.m: Dwight D. Eisenhower was a general before he became President.

44355.q: Which US President issued the most executive orders, more than 3,700?
44355.e: In his long term from 1933 to 1945, Roosevelt signed about 3,700 orders. No other President has come anywhere near this number.
44355.m: Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the most executive orders.

44356.q: Which number Congress of the United States met in January 2025?
44356.e: Each Congress lasts two years, counted from the first Congress of 1789. The 119th Congress sits from 2025 to 2027.
44356.m: Since January 2025 the 119th US Congress has been sitting.

44357.q: How many voting members does the US House of Representatives have (as of 2025)?
44357.e: The number 435 has applied since 1913 and was fixed by law in 1929. Every state has at least one seat.
44357.m: The US House of Representatives has 435 voting members.

44358.q: What is the title of the office that formally presides over the US Senate when the Vice President is absent?
44358.e: The President pro tempore is elected by the Senate; traditionally it is the longest-serving member of the majority party. This person is third in the presidential line of succession.
44358.m: Without the Vice President, the President pro tempore presides over the Senate.

44359.q: Who mainly decides which bills are put on the agenda in the US Senate?
44359.e: The Majority Leader is elected by the majority party and has priority to speak when business is planned. This lets him steer what the Senate debates.
44359.m: The Majority Leader shapes the Senate's agenda.

44360.q: What rights does the representative of Washington, D.C. have in the US House of Representatives?
a: They may take part in debate but not vote in the full House
44360.e: As well as the voting members, there are delegates for the capital and territories such as Puerto Rico. They work on committees but do not vote in the full House.
44360.m: The capital is represented in the House of Representatives without a vote in the full House.

44361.q: In which state did a disputed recount decide the winner of the 2000 presidential election?
44361.e: In Florida George W. Bush was only a few hundred votes ahead of Al Gore. In Bush v. Gore the Supreme Court stopped the recount, so Bush received Florida's electors.
44361.m: In 2000 the recount in Florida decided the presidential election.

44362.q: In the USA, what is it called when Congress successfully overrules a presidential veto?
44362.e: In a veto override, both chambers pass the rejected bill again with the required majority. It then becomes law without the President's signature.
44362.m: An overruled veto is called an override.

44363.q: Which Democratic President signed the Civil Rights Act against racial discrimination in 1964?
44363.e: Lyndon B. Johnson pushed the law through Congress after Kennedy's assassination. It banned discrimination on the grounds of colour, religion or origin.
44363.m: Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964.

44364.q: Which power of control held by the US Congress is called the “power of the purse”?
44364.e: Without the approval of Congress the government may not spend any money. This allows the legislature to restrict the executive effectively.
44364.m: With the power of the purse, Congress controls the government's money.

44365.q: With which power can the US President cancel the consequences of rulings by federal courts?
44365.e: Article II allows the President to grant pardons and reprieves for federal offences. Cases of impeachment are excluded.
44365.m: The US President may pardon federal offences.

44366.q: Since which amendment have US senators been elected directly by the people?
44366.e: Before 1913 the state legislatures elected the senators. The 17th Amendment introduced popular election.
44366.m: Since the 17th Amendment the people have elected senators directly.

a: Party officials who vote as delegates without a primary
44367.e: Superdelegates are, for example, members of Congress, governors and party leaders. Since 2018 they may no longer vote in the first ballot at the convention.
44367.m: Superdelegates are party figures who are delegates without a primary.

44368.q: On which day was the Basic Law of the Federal Republic of Germany promulgated?
44368.e: The Basic Law was promulgated in Bonn on 23 May 1949 and came into force at the end of that day. 23 May is therefore regarded as the birthday of the Federal Republic.
44368.m: The Basic Law was promulgated on 23 May 1949.

44369.q: Which body drew up the Basic Law in 1948/49?
44369.e: The Parliamentary Council met in Bonn and had 65 voting members sent by the state parliaments. Its president was Konrad Adenauer.
44369.m: The Parliamentary Council wrote the Basic Law in Bonn.

44370.q: With which sentence does Article 1 of the Basic Law begin?
a: All persons shall be equal before the law.
All state authority is derived from the people.
Freedom of the person shall be inviolable.
44370.e: Article 1 paragraph 1 places human dignity at the start of the constitution. This position is a deliberate response to the crimes of National Socialism.
44370.m: The Basic Law begins with the protection of human dignity.

44371.q: What is Article 79 paragraph 3 of the Basic Law called, which puts certain principles beyond any constitutional amendment?
44371.e: The eternity clause forbids amendments affecting the division of the federation into states or the principles of Articles 1 and 20. This is meant to prevent democracy from being abolished legally.
44371.m: The eternity clause protects the core of the Basic Law from any change.

44372.q: What majority does an amendment to the Basic Law need?
a: Two thirds in the Bundestag and Bundesrat
Three quarters in the Bundestag alone
A simple majority in both chambers
44372.e: Under Article 79 paragraph 2, an amendment must be approved by two thirds of the members of the Bundestag and two thirds of the votes of the Bundesrat. A referendum is not provided for.
44372.m: Amending the Basic Law needs two-thirds majorities in the Bundestag and Bundesrat.

44373.q: Why did the authors of the Basic Law deliberately not choose the name “constitution” in 1949?
a: Because of the division it was to be seen as provisional.
The Allies expressly banned the word.
A constitution would have required a monarchy.
The word had been reserved for Prussia since 1871.
44373.e: Because Germany was divided, the Basic Law was understood as a temporary order until reunification. Article 146 still provides that it can be replaced by a constitution adopted by the people.
44373.m: The Basic Law was originally meant as a provisional arrangement for a divided country.

44374.q: Under which article of the Basic Law did the GDR join the Federal Republic in 1990?
44374.e: The GDR's People's Chamber decided to join under the old Article 23, which allowed other parts of Germany to join. As a result the Basic Law applied to all of Germany from 3 October 1990.
44374.m: Reunification in 1990 took place as accession under the old Article 23.

44375.q: In which article does the Basic Law state that Germany is a democratic and social federal state?
44375.e: Article 20 contains the structural principles of the state: democracy, the welfare state, the federal state and the rule of law. Paragraph 4 also gives a right of resistance against anyone who tries to abolish this order.
44375.m: Article 20 names the basic principles of the German state.

44376.q: How long is a regular term of the German Bundestag?
44376.e: Under Article 39 of the Basic Law the Bundestag is elected for four years. An early election is only possible if the Federal President dissolves it.
44376.m: The Bundestag is elected for four years.

44377.q: Which office helps the Bundestag with parliamentary control of the armed forces?
a: The Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces
44377.e: The office of Parliamentary Commissioner for the Armed Forces is laid down in Article 45b of the Basic Law, and the holder is elected by the Bundestag. Since 2025 Henning Otte has held this office, and soldiers can contact him directly.
44377.m: The Parliamentary Commissioner helps the Bundestag control the armed forces.

44378.q: Which vote decides how seats are distributed among the parties in the Bundestag election?
44378.e: With the second vote you vote for a party's state list, and the distribution of seats in the Bundestag is based on this. With the first vote you vote for a person in the constituency.
44378.m: The second vote decides the strength of the parties in the Bundestag.

44379.q: Which instrument under Article 68 of the Basic Law have chancellors used several times to bring about early elections?
44379.e: If the chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Federal President can dissolve the Bundestag on the chancellor's proposal. This led to early elections in 2005 and at the end of 2024, for example.
44379.m: In Germany a lost confidence vote can lead to new elections.

44380.q: How many seats does the Bundestag have after the 2023 electoral reform (as of 2025)?
44380.e: The 2023 reform abolished overhang and balancing seats and fixed the size at 630 seats. Before that, the Bundestag had grown to 736 members in 2021.
44380.m: Since the 2023 reform the Bundestag has had 630 seats.

44381.q: What is the instrument called with which the Bundestag can only remove a chancellor by electing a successor?
44381.e: Under Article 67, the Bundestag must elect a new chancellor by majority to remove the old one. So far this has only succeeded in 1982, when Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt.
44381.m: In a constructive vote of no confidence a new chancellor must be elected at the same time.

44382.q: Under Article 63, who proposes a candidate for chancellor to the Bundestag?
44382.e: The Federal President proposes the person who has usually been chosen beforehand in coalition talks. The Bundestag then elects them without debate by a majority of its members.
44382.m: The Federal President proposes the chancellor and the Bundestag elects them.

44383.q: Who was elected President of the German Bundestag in March 2025?
44383.e: Julia Klöckner of the CDU was elected on 25 March 2025 at the opening session. She succeeded Bärbel Bas of the SPD.
44383.m: Since 2025 Julia Klöckner has presided over the Bundestag.

44384.q: Whom does the Bundesrat represent in German politics?
44384.e: Through the Bundesrat the states take part in federal lawmaking and administration. It is therefore a central body of German federalism.
44384.m: In the Bundesrat the states take part in federal politics.

44385.q: How are the members of the Bundesrat chosen?
a: They are sent by the state governments
They are elected directly by the people
They are elected by the Bundestag
They are appointed by the Federal President
44385.e: Members of the Bundesrat are members of the state governments, such as minister-presidents and state ministers. That is why there are no separate Bundesrat elections.
44385.m: The state governments send their members to the Bundesrat.

44386.q: Why do small states have more weight in the German Bundesrat in relation to their population than large ones?
a: Every state has at least three votes
All states have the same number of votes
The votes are drawn by lot
44386.e: The votes are only roughly graded by population, from three to six. A small state like Bremen has three, while large North Rhine-Westphalia has only six.
44386.m: Small states are over-represented in the Bundesrat.

44387.q: What is the minimum and maximum number of votes a state has in the Bundesrat?
44387.e: Article 51 gives every state at least three votes, and states with over 7 million inhabitants get six. Small states are therefore more strongly represented in relation to their population.
44387.m: Each state has between three and six votes in the Bundesrat.

44388.q: What applies to the way a state casts its votes in the Bundesrat?
a: Its votes must be cast as a block.
Each member votes freely according to conscience.
The votes are divided by party.
44388.e: Under Article 51 paragraph 3, a state can only cast its votes as a block. Divided coalitions in a state therefore often abstain, which in practice works like a no.
44388.m: A state must cast all its votes the same way in the Bundesrat.

44389.q: What are federal laws called that cannot be passed without the consent of the Bundesrat?
44389.e: For consent laws the Bundesrat has an absolute veto. For objection laws, the Bundestag can overrule an objection by the Bundesrat.
44389.m: Consent laws absolutely need the Bundesrat's yes.

44390.q: Which joint body looks for a compromise when the Bundestag and Bundesrat disagree on a law?
44390.e: The mediation committee has 16 members each from the Bundestag and the Bundesrat. It works out proposals for agreement, which both chambers then vote on.
44390.m: In disputes between the Bundestag and Bundesrat, the mediation committee mediates.

44391.q: What special task does the President of the Bundesrat have?
a: He deputises for the Federal President.
44391.e: If the Federal President is unable to act, the President of the Bundesrat exercises his powers under Article 57. The office rotates every year among the heads of the state governments.
44391.m: The President of the Bundesrat is the Federal President's deputy.

44392.q: In which city is the Federal Constitutional Court based?
44392.e: The Federal Constitutional Court has been in Karlsruhe since it was founded, where the Federal Court of Justice also is. “Karlsruhe” is therefore often used as a symbol for the court.
44392.m: The Federal Constitutional Court is based in Karlsruhe.

44393.q: In which year did the Federal Constitutional Court start work?
44393.e: The court was set up under the Federal Constitutional Court Act and began work on 28 September 1951. So it started a good two years after the Basic Law.
44393.m: The Federal Constitutional Court has been working since 1951.

44394.q: How is the Federal Constitutional Court organised?
a: Two senates of eight judges each
Three senates of five judges each
Four chambers of four judges each
44394.e: The court has 16 judges divided between two senates. For simpler cases the senates form smaller chambers of three members each.
44394.m: The Federal Constitutional Court has two senates of eight judges each.

44395.q: For how long are judges of the Federal Constitutional Court elected?
44395.e: The term is twelve years and ends at the latest at the age of 68. Ruling out re-election is meant to strengthen the judges' independence.
44395.m: Constitutional judges serve twelve years and may not be re-elected.

44396.q: Who elects the judges of the Federal Constitutional Court?
a: The Bundestag and Bundesrat, half each
The presidents of the federal courts
44396.e: The Bundestag and the Bundesrat each elect half of the judges, by a two-thirds majority. This means government and opposition usually have to agree on candidates.
44396.m: The Bundestag and Bundesrat each elect half of the constitutional judges.

44397.q: With which procedure can any person go to the Federal Constitutional Court if they feel their fundamental rights have been violated?
44397.e: The constitutional complaint is open to anyone who claims a violation of their fundamental rights by public authority. Usually all other legal remedies must be used first.
44397.m: With a constitutional complaint, citizens defend their fundamental rights in Karlsruhe.

44398.q: Which two parties did the Federal Constitutional Court ban in the 1950s?
44398.e: The court banned the neo-Nazi Socialist Reich Party in 1952 and the Communist Party of Germany in 1956. There have been no further party bans since.
44398.m: In the 1950s the SRP and the KPD were banned.

44399.q: Who can apply to the Federal Constitutional Court for abstract judicial review?
a: A quarter of the members of the Bundestag
44399.e: Those entitled to apply are the federal government, a state government or a quarter of the members of the Bundestag. A law is reviewed independently of a specific dispute.
44399.m: Abstract judicial review examines a law without a specific case.

44400.q: In Austria, who appoints the chancellor after the National Council election?
a: The National Council by secret ballot
44400.e: In Austria the Federal President appoints the chancellor and, on the chancellor's proposal, the government. But the government needs the confidence of the majority in the National Council, which has had 183 members since 1971.
44400.m: In Austria the Federal President appoints the chancellor.

44401.q: How long has a legislative term of the Austrian National Council lasted since 2007?
44401.e: The 2007 electoral reform extended the legislative term from four to five years. Early dissolution remains possible.
44401.m: Since 2007 the National Council has been elected for five years.

44402.q: Since 2007, from what age can you vote in National Council elections in Austria?
44402.e: In 2007 Austria lowered the voting age to 16. It was the first EU country with a voting age of 16 at national level.
44402.m: In Austria you can vote for the National Council at 16.

44403.q: How high is the threshold in Austrian National Council elections?
44403.e: A party needs at least 4 per cent of the valid votes nationwide or a basic seat in a regional constituency. The hurdle is therefore lower than in Germany.
44403.m: In Austria the threshold for the National Council is four per cent.

44404.q: Which body do the National Council and Federal Council form together in Austria, for example for the swearing-in of the Federal President?
44404.e: When the National Council meets together with the Federal Council, the Federal Assembly is formed. The newly elected Federal President takes his oath before it.
44404.m: The National Council and Federal Council together form the Federal Assembly.

44405.q: What happened in the Austrian National Council in May 2019 for the first time in the Second Republic?
a: A government was removed by a vote of no confidence.
A Federal President was voted out.
44405.e: After the Ibiza affair, the National Council passed a vote of no confidence in the Kurz government on 27 May 2019. A caretaker government under Brigitte Bierlein then ran the country.
44405.m: In May 2019 the National Council toppled a government by a vote of no confidence for the first time.

44406.q: Which party became the strongest force for the first time in the 2024 National Council election?
44406.e: The FPÖ won about 29 per cent of the vote in the election of 29 September 2024. However, the government was then formed by the ÖVP, SPÖ and NEOS.
44406.m: In 2024 the FPÖ became the strongest party in the National Council for the first time.

44407.q: What model does the parliament building on Vienna's Ringstrasse recall?
44407.e: The architect Theophil Hansen designed the building in the style of ancient Greece, the cradle of democracy. It was completed in 1883 and reopened in 2023 after renovation.
44407.m: The Vienna parliament recalls a Greek temple.

44408.q: How is the Austrian Federal President chosen?
44408.e: Since 1951 the people have elected the Federal President directly. In Germany, by contrast, the Federal Convention elects the President.
44408.m: In Austria the people elect the Federal President directly.

44409.q: How long is a term of office of the Austrian Federal President?
44409.e: The term is six years, and immediate re-election is allowed only once. So one person can be in office for a maximum of twelve years in a row.
44409.m: The Austrian Federal President serves for six years.

44410.q: What happens if nobody wins an absolute majority in the first round of the Austrian presidential election?
a: A run-off between the top two
Lots are drawn among all of them
44410.e: Whoever gets more than half of the valid votes is elected. Otherwise the two candidates with the most votes face each other in a run-off.
44410.m: Without an absolute majority there is a run-off between the top two.

44411.q: Who has been Austria's Federal President since 2017 (as of 2025)?
44411.e: Alexander Van der Bellen took office on 26 January 2017. In 2022 he was re-elected in the first round.
44411.m: Alexander Van der Bellen has been Austria's Federal President since 2017.

44412.q: Why did the 2016 run-off for Federal President have to be repeated?
a: The Constitutional Court annulled it because of procedural errors.
Both candidates got exactly the same number of votes.
A candidate withdrew shortly before the vote.
44412.e: In July 2016 the Constitutional Court annulled the run-off because of irregularities in counting the postal votes. Van der Bellen won the repeat vote in December 2016.
44412.m: The 2016 run-off was repeated because of errors with the postal vote.

44413.q: What important power does the Austrian Federal President have over the government?
a: He appoints and dismisses the chancellor.
He chooses the members of parliament.
44413.e: Under Article 70 of the Federal Constitutional Law, the Federal President appoints the chancellor and, on the chancellor's proposal, the ministers. He can also dismiss the government.
44413.m: In Austria the Federal President appoints the chancellor.

44414.q: What power does the Austrian Federal President have over the National Council?
a: He can block its laws permanently without reason
44414.e: The Federal President can dissolve the National Council, after which new elections follow. But he may only use this power once for the same reason.
44414.m: The Austrian Federal President can dissolve the National Council.

44415.q: In which building does the Austrian Federal President have his official seat?
44415.e: The Presidential Chancellery is in the Leopoldine Wing of the Vienna Hofburg. The Federal Chancellery sits opposite on the Ballhausplatz.
44415.m: The Federal President works in the Vienna Hofburg.

44416.q: How does the Liechtenstein constitution describe the country's form of state?
a: Constitutional hereditary monarchy on a democratic basis
Parliamentary elective monarchy with a federal council
Absolute monarchy with an advisory parliament
Princely republic with a representative assembly
44416.e: Article 2 calls the principality a constitutional hereditary monarchy on a democratic and parliamentary basis. State power lies with the Prince and the people.
44416.m: In Liechtenstein the Prince and the people share state power.

44417.q: From which year does Liechtenstein's constitution date, which was revised in 2003?
44417.e: The constitution of 5 October 1921 clearly strengthened the rights of the people for the first time. It is still in force but has been amended several times, most of all in 2003.

44418.q: How was the 2003 constitutional revision adopted in Liechtenstein?
a: In a referendum with almost two thirds voting yes
By a decision of parliament alone
By a decree of the Prince without a vote
By a vote in the Council of Europe
44418.e: On 16 March 2003 about 64 per cent of voters approved the initiative of the princely house. This strengthened the Prince's position overall.
44418.m: The people of Liechtenstein approved the constitutional revision at the ballot box in 2003.

44419.q: What right did the people of Liechtenstein gain with the 2003 constitutional revision?
a: They can abolish the monarchy by initiative.
They elect the Prince every ten years.
They can no longer dissolve parliament.
44419.e: Since 2003 a popular initiative can start a procedure to abolish the monarchy. In addition, the people can bring a motion of no confidence against the Prince.
44419.m: Since 2003 the people of Liechtenstein could abolish the monarchy.

44420.q: What did the Council of Europe's Venice Commission criticise about Liechtenstein's 2003 constitutional revision?
a: It strengthened the Prince's power too much
44420.e: The Venice Commission advises states on constitutional matters. It criticised the revision for extending the Prince's power over the other organs of state.
44420.m: The Council of Europe's Venice Commission criticised the 2003 revision.

44421.q: How many members does the parliament (Landtag) of the Principality of Liechtenstein have?
44421.e: The Landtag has 25 members, elected every four years. Of these, 15 come from the Oberland and 10 from the Unterland.

44422.q: What did the people of Liechtenstein decide in 2012 about the Prince's veto?
a: They limited the veto to taxes.
They transferred the veto to parliament.
44422.e: The popular initiative wanted to prevent the Prince from overturning popular votes with his veto. About three quarters of voters rejected it on 1 July 2012.
44422.m: The Prince's veto remained after a referendum in 2012.

44423.q: Who has carried out the duties of head of state in Liechtenstein as the Prince's deputy since 2004?
44423.e: Prince Hans-Adam II appointed his son Alois as his deputy on 15 August 2004. Hans-Adam II formally remains head of state.
44423.m: Hereditary Prince Alois has carried out the duties of head of state since 2004.

44424.q: In which year was the constitution of the French Fifth Republic adopted?
44424.e: The constitution was adopted by referendum in September 1958 and promulgated on 4 October 1958. It replaced the unstable Fourth Republic.
44424.m: The Fifth Republic begins with the constitution of 1958.

44425.q: Which crisis led to Charles de Gaulle's return and the founding of the Fifth Republic in 1958?
44425.e: A coup by French military officers in Algiers brought the Fourth Republic to the brink of civil war. De Gaulle became head of government and had a new constitution drawn up.
44425.m: The Algerian crisis brought de Gaulle back to power in 1958.

44426.q: What does political science usually call the system of government of the Fifth Republic?
44426.e: A directly elected president with wide powers stands alongside a prime minister who depends on parliament. This dual leadership characterises the semi-presidential system.
44426.m: France has a semi-presidential system with a president and a prime minister.

44427.q: Since when has the French President been elected directly by the people?
44427.e: At first an electoral college elected the President. In 1962 de Gaulle pushed through direct election by referendum, and the first such election took place in 1965.
44427.m: Since 1962 the French have elected their President directly.

44428.q: What was changed about the presidency in France by the referendum of 2000?
a: The term fell from seven to five years.
The term rose from five to seven years.
44428.e: With the so-called quinquennat, the term was shortened to five years from 2002. Since 2008, a maximum of two consecutive terms has also been allowed.
44428.m: Since 2002 the French President's term has lasted five years.

44429.q: Which office is particularly powerful in the French Fifth Republic?
a: The President of the Constitutional Council
44429.e: The 1958 constitution was tailored to Charles de Gaulle. The President appoints the Prime Minister, can dissolve the National Assembly and has emergency powers.
44429.m: In France the President has a very strong position.

44430.q: Which article of the constitution allows the French government to push a law through without a vote, provided no motion of censure succeeds?
44430.e: With “49.3” the government links a law to a question of confidence. If the following motion of censure fails, the law is considered adopted.
44430.m: With Article 49.3 France's government can pass a law without a vote.

44431.q: What is the task of the French Conseil constitutionnel?
a: It checks laws for their constitutionality
44431.e: The Conseil constitutionnel checks whether laws are compatible with the constitution and oversees national elections. It is comparable to a constitutional court.
44431.m: The Conseil constitutionnel watches over the French constitution.

44432.q: What is the main task of the Assemblée nationale in France?
a: It passes laws and scrutinises the government
It elects the President of the Republic
It rules as the supreme court
44432.e: The Assemblée nationale is the directly elected chamber of the French parliament. It passes laws and can bring down the government with a motion of censure.
44432.m: The Assemblée nationale makes laws and scrutinises the government.

44433.q: In which Paris building does the Assemblée nationale sit?
44433.e: The National Assembly sits in the Palais Bourbon on the Seine. The Senate sits in the Palais du Luxembourg, the President in the Élysée Palace.
44433.m: The Assemblée nationale sits in the Palais Bourbon.

44434.q: Under which electoral system are the members of the Assemblée nationale elected?
44434.e: Voting takes place in single-member constituencies; anyone who does not win an absolute majority in the first round must go to a second round. There a relative majority is enough.
44434.m: France elects its members of parliament by two-round majority voting.

44435.q: What does a candidate for the Assemblée nationale need to be elected in the first round?
a: An absolute majority of the votes
At least 5 per cent of the votes
44435.e: In the first round, whoever gets more than half of the votes and reaches a minimum turnout is elected. Otherwise there is a second round, in which a relative majority is enough.
44435.m: In the first round in France, an absolute majority is needed.

44436.q: What is the second chamber of the French parliament called, alongside the Assemblée nationale?
44436.e: The Senate is elected indirectly by about 160,000 electors, mainly municipal councillors. In case of disagreement, the Assemblée nationale usually has the last word.
44436.m: Besides the Assemblée nationale, France has the Senate.

44437.q: Who may dissolve the Assemblée nationale?
44437.e: Under Article 12 the President can dissolve the National Assembly, after which no further dissolution is allowed for a year. Emmanuel Macron did this in June 2024 after the European election.
44437.m: Only the French President can dissolve the Assemblée nationale.

44438.q: What happened in the Assemblée nationale in December 2024 for the first time since 1962?
a: A government was toppled by a motion of censure.
The President gave a speech there.
A woman became president of parliament.
44438.e: On 4 December 2024 the National Assembly passed a motion of censure against Michel Barnier's government. This had last happened in 1962, to the Pompidou government.
44438.m: In December 2024 the Assemblée nationale toppled the Barnier government.

44439.q: How long is a regular term in the Assemblée nationale?
44439.e: Members are elected for five years unless the President dissolves the chamber earlier. Since 2002 the elections have usually come shortly after the presidential election.
44439.m: Members of the Assemblée nationale are elected for five years.

44440.q: Where does the Westminster system get its name from?
a: From the Palace of Westminster in London
From the Treaty of Westminster of 1654
From the first Prime Minister, Westminster
44440.e: Both chambers of the British Parliament sit in the Palace of Westminster. The model of government that developed there was later adopted by many Commonwealth countries.
44440.m: The Westminster system is named after the London parliament building.

44441.q: Which electoral system is typical of House of Commons elections in Britain's Westminster system?
a: Relative majority voting in single-member constituencies
44441.e: Under “first past the post”, whoever gets the most votes wins in each constituency. This favours big parties and clear majorities.
44441.m: In the House of Commons, whoever gets the most votes wins each constituency.

44442.q: Who usually becomes Prime Minister in the Westminster system?
a: The leader of the majority party
The person with the most votes in the country
The oldest member of the House of Commons
44442.e: The monarch formally appoints whoever has the confidence of the House of Commons. That is normally the leader of the majority party.
44442.m: Whoever leads the majority in the House of Commons becomes Prime Minister.

44443.q: What is the body of the largest opposition party that mirrors the members of the government called?
44443.e: The official opposition names a spokesperson for each ministry. That way an alternative government stands ready.
44443.m: In the Westminster system the opposition forms a shadow cabinet.

44444.q: Which of these countries has a system of government based on the Westminster model?
44444.e: Canada, Australia, New Zealand and India adopted the British model with a government responsible to parliament. Switzerland, by contrast, has a directorial system.
44444.m: Canada is governed according to the Westminster model.

44445.q: On which day of the week does Prime Minister's Questions take place in the British House of Commons?
44445.e: Since 1997 the Prime Minister has answered MPs' questions for half an hour every Wednesday while Parliament is sitting. The clashes with the Leader of the Opposition are often heated.
44445.m: Prime Minister's Questions takes place on Wednesday.

44446.q: What role does the Speaker of the British House of Commons have?
a: He chairs debates in a politically neutral way.
He is the Prime Minister's deputy.
He represents the monarch in Parliament.
44446.e: After being elected, the Speaker leaves his party and chairs the sittings impartially. He calls for order, for example, with “Order!”.
44446.m: The Speaker chairs the House of Commons impartially.

44447.q: What is the wool-stuffed cushion called on which the presiding officer of the House of Lords sits?
44447.e: The Woolsack was introduced in the Middle Ages and is a reminder of how important the wool trade was for England. Today it is stuffed with wool from several Commonwealth countries.
44447.m: The presiding officer of the House of Lords sits on the Woolsack.

44448.q: What did the House of Lords Act 1999 do?
a: Most hereditary peers lost their seats.
The Lords were elected for the first time.
The House of Lords was abolished.
44448.e: The Act removed the automatic right of most hereditary peers to sit. As a compromise, 92 of them were allowed to stay for the time being; a further law of 2026 ends their right to sit as well.
44448.m: The House of Lords Act 1999 took away most hereditary peers' seats in the Lords.

44449.q: What are the 26 bishops of the Church of England who sit in the House of Lords called?
44449.e: The Lords Spiritual include the Archbishops of Canterbury and York. All other members are called Lords Temporal.
44449.m: The bishops in the House of Lords are called Lords Spiritual.

44450.q: Since the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, what power does the House of Lords have over most laws?
a: It cannot debate them at all.
44450.e: The Lords can hold up ordinary bills for about a year at most, and money bills for only a month. After that the House of Commons can pass them even without the Lords' consent.
44450.m: The House of Lords can only delay laws, not stop them.

44451.q: Which institution took over the House of Lords' role as the highest court in 2009?
a: Supreme Court of the United Kingdom
44451.e: The Constitutional Reform Act 2005 separated the judiciary and the legislature more clearly. The Supreme Court began work in October 2009.
44451.m: Since 2009 the Supreme Court has been the highest court in the UK.

44452.q: Who has presided over the sittings of the House of Lords since 2006?
44452.e: In the past the Lord Chancellor, a member of the government, presided over the sittings. Since 2006 the Lords have elected their own Lord Speaker.
44452.m: Since 2006 the House of Lords has been chaired by the Lord Speaker.

44453.q: What does the Salisbury Convention say?
a: The Lords do not block the government's election promises.
The Lords may not raise taxes.
The Prime Minister must come from the House of Lords.
44453.e: Under this constitutional convention, the Lords do not reject bills that were announced in the governing party's election manifesto. It arose in 1945 under the Labour government.
44453.m: The Salisbury Convention protects the government's election promises from the House of Lords.

44454.q: What is special about the constitution of the United Kingdom?
a: There is no single constitutional document.
It was only written down in 1999.
Only the monarch can change it.
44454.e: The British constitution is made up of laws, court rulings, conventions and customs. That is why it is often called unwritten, even though much of it is written down.
44454.m: Britain has no constitution in one single document.

44455.q: Which document of 1215 is regarded as an early foundation of British civil liberties?
44455.e: Magna Carta limited the power of King John. It is still a symbol today that even the ruler is bound by law.
44455.m: Magna Carta of 1215 limited the king's power.

44456.q: Which act of 1689 secured the rights of Parliament against the Crown after the Glorious Revolution?
44456.e: The Bill of Rights came about after James II was driven out and tied the Crown to Parliament's consent on important matters. It is still part of the British constitution today.
44456.m: The Bill of Rights of 1689 strengthened Parliament against the king.

44457.q: Which principle states that the British Parliament can make or repeal any law?
44457.e: According to the jurist A. V. Dicey, no Parliament can bind its successors, and no court can declare an Act of Parliament invalid. This is a core principle of the British constitution.
44457.m: In the United Kingdom, Parliament is sovereign.

44458.q: What are unwritten but strictly followed rules called, such as the monarch's duty to sign laws?
44458.e: Constitutional conventions are politically binding but cannot be enforced in court. They govern, for example, that the monarch acts on the government's advice.
44458.m: Constitutional conventions are unwritten rules of British politics.

44459.q: When did a British monarch last refuse royal assent to a law?
44459.e: In 1708 Queen Anne refused assent to the Scottish Militia Bill. Since then royal assent has always been given according to a fixed convention.
44459.m: Since 1708 no British monarch has rejected a law.

44460.q: Which act of 1998 made the European Convention on Human Rights directly applicable in British courts?
44460.e: Since the Human Rights Act 1998, people can rely directly on the ECHR in British courts. But courts may not strike down a law, only declare it incompatible.
44460.m: In 1998 the Human Rights Act brought the ECHR into British law.

44461.q: What were the corruption investigations from 1992 called that made Italy's old party system collapse?
44461.e: The Milan investigations “Mani pulite” (clean hands) uncovered a system of bribes known as Tangentopoli. Major parties such as the Democrazia Cristiana then dissolved.
44461.m: From 1992 the “Mani pulite” investigations ended Italy's old party system.

44462.q: Which feature of the Italian parliament is seen as one cause of frequent changes of government?
a: The government needs the confidence of both chambers.
The Senate is appointed by the President.
44462.e: In perfect bicameralism the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate have equal rights. If the government loses its majority in just one chamber, it can fall.
44462.m: In Italy the government must have the confidence of both chambers.

44463.q: Roughly how many governments has Italy had since 1946 (as of 2025)?
44463.e: Giorgia Meloni's government is the 68th government of the Republic. On average a government has therefore lasted only just over a year.
44463.m: Italy has had almost 70 governments since 1946.

44464.q: Who became Italy's first woman prime minister in October 2022?
44464.e: Giorgia Meloni of Fratelli d'Italia formed a centre-right government after the 2022 election. She is the first woman to head an Italian government.
44464.m: Since 2022 Giorgia Meloni has been Italy's first woman prime minister.

44465.q: Which former President of the European Central Bank led a government of national unity from 2021 to 2022?
44465.e: Mario Draghi became prime minister of a broad all-party government in February 2021. He resigned in July 2022 after coalition partners withdrew their support.
44465.m: Mario Draghi led Italy as a non-party head of government from 2021 to 2022.

44466.q: What happened in Italy after the failed constitutional referendum of December 2016?
44466.e: Matteo Renzi wanted to greatly reduce the size and power of the Senate to make governments more stable. About 59 per cent voted no, after which Renzi resigned.
44466.m: After the no vote in 2016, Matteo Renzi resigned.

44467.q: What did Italians decide in the 2020 referendum?
a: The number of members of parliament was reduced.
The voting age was lowered to 16.
44467.e: The Chamber of Deputies was reduced from 630 to 400 seats, and the Senate from 315 to 200 elected senators. The change applied from the 2022 election.
44467.m: Since 2022 Italy's parliament has had far fewer members.

44469.q: How many clauses of Magna Carta are still in force in the United Kingdom today?
44469.e: Most clauses were repealed in the 19th and 20th centuries. Only three are still in force, including those on the freedoms of the Church and the rights of the City of London.
44469.m: Only a few clauses of Magna Carta are still law.

44470.q: Which charter was issued in 1217 as an addition to Magna Carta and regulated the use of royal forests?
44470.e: The Charter of the Forest gave free people access to royal forests again, for example to graze pigs and collect wood.
44470.m: The Charter of the Forest added to Magna Carta in 1217.

44471.q: Which social group forced Magna Carta on the king?
44471.e: The noble landowners rose up against the king and forced him to make concessions. At first the charter mainly protected their rights.
44471.m: Magna Carta was originally an agreement between the king and the nobility.

44472.q: Which principle of Magna Carta is regarded as a forerunner of the right to a fair trial?
a: Free choice of where to live
44472.e: One clause stated that no free man may be arrested or punished except by the lawful judgement of his equals or by the law of the land.
44472.m: Magna Carta required punishments to be imposed only according to law and judgement.

44473.q: What promise about justice does the king make in Magna Carta?
a: He will sell justice to no one
He will give everyone a horse
He will hold elections every year
44473.e: One clause says, roughly: to no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice.
44473.m: According to Magna Carta, justice may be neither bought nor delayed.

44474.q: Where are two of the surviving originals of the 1215 Magna Carta kept?
a: In the British Library in London
In the Vatican Museums in Rome
In the Library of Congress in Washington
44474.e: Four originals from 1215 survive. Two are in the British Library, and one each in Lincoln and Salisbury cathedrals.
44474.m: Two originals of Magna Carta are in the British Library.

44475.q: Which principle did Magna Carta write down for the first time?
a: Even the king is bound by the law
All people are equal from birth
The Church is under the king
44475.e: Magna Carta limited the king's power and bound him to law and custom. It was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225 and is regarded as an important step towards the rule of law.
44475.m: Magna Carta put the king under the law.

44476.q: In which year did the English Parliament pass the Habeas Corpus Act?
44476.e: The act set out in more detail an older legal remedy against arbitrary imprisonment. It is regarded as a milestone in protecting personal freedom.
44476.m: The Habeas Corpus Act dates from 1679.

44477.q: What does the Latin phrase “habeas corpus” literally mean?
44477.e: The formula comes from the writ ordering the jailer to bring the prisoner before the court in person.
44477.m: Habeas corpus literally means that the body must be produced.

44478.q: What does the Habeas Corpus Act mainly protect against?
44478.e: The act was meant to prevent people from being held for as long as anyone liked without reason or trial. The lawfulness of detention must be checked quickly.
44478.m: Habeas corpus protects people from detention without control by a judge.

44479.q: Under which English king was the Habeas Corpus Act passed?
44479.e: Charles II reigned after the restoration of the monarchy. Parliament wanted to use the act to prevent arbitrary arrests by the Crown.
44479.m: The Habeas Corpus Act was passed in the reign of Charles II.

44480.q: Which US President partly suspended habeas corpus in 1861 during the Civil War?
44480.e: In April 1861 Lincoln had habeas corpus suspended in parts of Maryland to prevent sabotage against the Union. The US Constitution only allows suspension in cases of rebellion or invasion.
44480.m: Even Abraham Lincoln temporarily suspended habeas corpus during the war.

44481.q: In Switzerland, what right does a person have who is taken into pre-trial detention?
a: To be brought before a court quickly
44481.e: The Federal Constitution (Art. 31) requires that a person in pre-trial detention be brought before a court without delay. The court checks whether the detention is lawful.
44481.m: The Federal Constitution guarantees a quick review by a court in case of detention.

44482.q: Which international treaty also protects against arbitrary detention in Europe?
a: The European Convention on Human Rights
44482.e: The ECHR guarantees the right to liberty and security. Every person arrested is entitled to have their detention reviewed by a court, in Switzerland too.
44482.m: The ECHR protects personal freedom against arbitrary detention.

44483.q: Which royal couple accepted the English crown in 1689 together with the Bill of Rights?
a: James II and Mary of Modena
44483.e: After James II fled, Parliament offered the crown to William of Orange and his wife Mary. In return they had to accept the rights set down in the Bill of Rights.
44483.m: William III and Mary II became monarchs on the terms of the Bill of Rights.

44484.q: Which right of subjects towards the king did the Bill of Rights confirm?
a: The right to choose a profession freely
44484.e: Subjects may approach the king with petitions without being prosecuted for it.
44484.m: The right to petition has one root in the English Bill of Rights.

44485.q: Which people did the Bill of Rights exclude from the succession to the English throne?
44485.e: After the experience with the Catholic King James II, Catholics and people married to Catholics were no longer allowed to take the throne.
44485.m: The Bill of Rights secured a Protestant succession to the throne.

44486.q: According to the Bill of Rights, what does the monarch need Parliament's consent for?
44486.e: The Bill of Rights declared taxes without Parliament's approval illegal. This gave Parliament control over the budget.
44486.m: Without Parliament the king could no longer raise taxes.

44487.q: What did the Bill of Rights demand for the election of members of Parliament?
44487.e: The Bill of Rights stated that the election of members of Parliament ought to be free. The king was not allowed to interfere.
44487.m: Free parliamentary elections are among the demands of the Bill of Rights.

44488.q: What did the Bill of Rights forbid in peacetime without Parliament's consent?
44488.e: A standing army in peacetime could only be kept with Parliament's consent. This was so that the king could not use an army against the people.
44488.m: The Bill of Rights put the military under parliamentary control.

44489.q: Which punishments did the English Bill of Rights expressly forbid?
44489.e: The wording “cruel and unusual punishments” was later taken over into the Eighth Amendment to the US Constitution.
44489.m: Cruel and unusual punishments were forbidden by the Bill of Rights.

44490.q: Which group of people did the Bill of Rights expressly allow to have arms for their defence?
44490.e: James II had disarmed Protestants. The Bill of Rights allowed them arms for their defence again, as permitted by law.
44490.m: The Bill of Rights gave Protestants back the right to arms for their defence.

44491.q: In which year was the Virginia Declaration of Rights adopted?
44491.e: The Virginia Convention adopted the declaration in June 1776, even before the United States Declaration of Independence.
44491.m: The Virginia Declaration of Rights dates from 1776.

44492.q: Who is regarded as the main author of the Virginia Declaration of Rights?
44492.e: George Mason, a planter and politician from Virginia, drafted most of the text.
44492.m: George Mason wrote the draft of the Virginia Declaration of Rights.

44493.q: Why is the Virginia Declaration of Rights regarded as especially important?
a: First modern bill of fundamental rights
44493.e: For the first time it set out the inborn, inalienable rights of all people in a binding state document.
44493.m: The Virginia Declaration is regarded as the first modern declaration of human rights.

44494.q: Which basic principle of state power does the Virginia Declaration of Rights name?
a: All power comes from the people
All power lies with the governor
The Church stands above the state
44494.e: The declaration states that all power is vested in the people and that officials are answerable to them. This is the principle of popular sovereignty.
44494.m: The Virginia Declaration is based on popular sovereignty.

44495.q: Which later document did the Virginia Declaration of Rights directly influence?
44495.e: The first ten amendments to the US Constitution of 1791 adopted many phrases from Virginia, for example on freedom of the press and religion.
44495.m: The Virginia Declaration was a model for the American Bill of Rights.

44496.q: Which contradiction does the Virginia Declaration of Rights show from today's point of view?
a: It did not apply to slaves
It gave the vote only to women
44496.e: Although all people were described as free by nature, slavery remained in Virginia. George Mason himself kept slaves.
44496.m: The rights of freedom of 1776 did not apply to enslaved people.

44497.q: Which freedom did the Virginia Declaration of Rights call “one of the great bulwarks of liberty”?
44497.e: The declaration states that the freedom of the press is one of the great bulwarks of liberty and can only be restrained by despotic governments.
44497.m: As early as 1776 freedom of the press was seen as a protection of liberty.

44498.q: How does Article 1 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen begin in French?
a: Les hommes naissent et demeurent libres et égaux en droits
Le peuple est souverain et indivisible
44498.e: Article 1 declares that people are born and remain free and equal in rights. Social distinctions may only be based on the common good.
44498.m: According to Article 1, all people are free and equal in rights from birth.

44499.q: Which French general introduced a first draft of the Declaration and was influenced by the American model?
44499.e: La Fayette had fought in the American War of Independence and worked with Thomas Jefferson on the draft.
44499.m: La Fayette linked the American and French ideas of human rights.

44500.q: How does the Declaration of 1789 describe property?
a: As an inviolable and sacred right
As a privilege of the nobility
As the possession of the state
As a right of the Church
44500.e: Article 17 calls property an inviolable and sacred right. Expropriation is only allowed in case of public necessity and with fair compensation.
44500.m: Property was especially strongly protected in 1789.

44501.q: How does Article 6 of the Declaration of 1789 define the law?
a: As the expression of the general will
As the custom of the ancestors
44501.e: The formula “La loi est l'expression de la volonté générale” goes back to Jean-Jacques Rousseau. All citizens may take part in making laws.
44501.m: After 1789 the law is the expression of the will of the people.

44502.q: What status does the Declaration of 1789 have in French law today?
a: It is part of constitutional law
It is just a museum piece
44502.e: The preamble of the 1958 constitution refers to the Declaration. The Constitutional Council also checks laws against it.
44502.m: The Declaration of 1789 is still constitutional law in France today.

44503.q: Which principle of the separation of powers does Article 16 of the Declaration of 1789 stress?
a: No separation of powers, no constitution
The king stands above the law
44503.e: Article 16 says that a society in which rights are not guaranteed and powers not separated has no constitution.
44503.m: Separation of powers and fundamental rights belong to every true constitution.

44504.q: In which city was the European Convention on Human Rights signed in 1950?
44504.e: The member states of the Council of Europe signed the Convention in Rome on 4 November 1950.
44504.m: The ECHR was signed in Rome in 1950.

44505.q: Which international organisation is behind the European Convention on Human Rights?
44505.e: The ECHR is a treaty of the Council of Europe, which was founded in 1949. It must be distinguished from the European Union.
44505.m: The ECHR belongs to the Council of Europe, not the EU.

44506.q: Which fundamental right does Article 3 of the ECHR protect without any exception?
44506.e: Article 3 forbids torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. The ban is absolute, even in war or a state of emergency.
44506.m: The ECHR's ban on torture has no exceptions.

44507.q: What condition must an individual usually meet before they can bring a complaint in Strasbourg?
a: Use up all domestic legal remedies
The consent of their own government
44507.e: The Court only examines a case if it has first gone through all national courts. In Switzerland that is usually the Federal Supreme Court.
44507.m: Before going to Strasbourg you must go through the courts in your own country.

44508.q: Which right does the ECHR guarantee with, among other things, the presumption of innocence and an independent court?
a: The right to a fair trial
44508.e: Art. 6 ECHR ensures an independent court, a public hearing within a reasonable time and the presumption of innocence.
44508.m: The ECHR guarantees a fair trial.

44509.q: Which Swiss association won a climate case before the European Court of Human Rights in 2024?
44509.e: In April 2024 the Court found that Switzerland had violated Art. 8 ECHR through insufficient climate protection.
44509.m: With the KlimaSeniorinnen ruling, the Court found a breach of the ECHR because of insufficient climate protection for the first time.

44510.q: What does Protocol No. 13 to the ECHR, which Switzerland has also ratified, forbid?
a: The death penalty in all circumstances
The death penalty only in peacetime
44510.e: Protocol No. 6 at first banned the death penalty only in peacetime. Protocol No. 13 bans it without exception, so in war too.
44510.m: Protocol No. 13 bans the death penalty without exception.

44511.q: Where are the fundamental rights found in the Swiss Federal Constitution?
a: Near the beginning, after the general provisions
Right at the end in the transitional provisions
Nowhere, only in the Civil Code
44511.e: After the general provisions, Title 2 contains the list of fundamental rights (Art. 7 to 36). It begins with human dignity.
44511.m: The fundamental rights are near the front of the Federal Constitution.

44512.q: With which fundamental right does the list of fundamental rights in the Federal Constitution begin, in Art. 7?
44512.e: Art. 7 of the Federal Constitution reads: “Human dignity must be respected and protected.” It is the basis of all other fundamental rights.
44512.m: Human dignity is at the start of the list of fundamental rights.

44513.q: What does Art. 10 para. 1 of the Federal Constitution expressly forbid?
44513.e: Art. 10 of the Federal Constitution protects the right to life. Paragraph 1 states that the death penalty is prohibited.
44513.m: The Federal Constitution forbids the death penalty.

44514.q: Which fundamental right protects the use of your own mother tongue?
44514.e: Freedom of language (Art. 18 of the Federal Constitution) protects the use of your own language, especially your mother tongue, in private life.
44514.m: Everyone in Switzerland may use their own language.

44515.q: Which social right does Art. 19 of the Federal Constitution guarantee?
44515.e: The cantons must offer all children adequate basic education free of charge.
44515.m: Under the constitution, basic education in Switzerland is free.

44516.q: Which fundamental right in the Federal Constitution is reserved for Swiss citizens only?
44516.e: Art. 24 of the Federal Constitution allows Swiss nationals to settle anywhere in the country and to leave the country. For others, laws and agreements apply.
44516.m: Freedom of residence is a civil right of Swiss citizens.

44517.q: What does Art. 35 of the Federal Constitution require of everyone who carries out state tasks?
a: They are bound by fundamental rights
44517.e: Art. 35 of the Federal Constitution requires that fundamental rights be upheld throughout the legal system. Anyone who carries out state tasks must respect them and help put them into practice.
44517.m: Anyone who carries out state tasks must respect fundamental rights.

44518.q: Why can the Federal Supreme Court not strike down a federal act even if it violates fundamental rights?
a: Federal acts are binding under Art. 190 of the Federal Constitution
Federal acts only apply for a limited time
The Federal Supreme Court is only responsible for criminal law
Federal acts are subject to the UN
44518.e: Art. 190 of the Federal Constitution obliges the courts to apply federal acts. Switzerland therefore has no constitutional review of federal acts.
44518.m: Courts must apply federal acts, even if they are problematic.

44519.q: Which fundamental right does Art. 17 of the Federal Constitution protect, banning censorship?
44519.e: Art. 17 of the Federal Constitution guarantees the freedom of the press, radio and television, bans censorship and protects editorial secrecy.
44519.m: Media freedom protects the press, radio and television from censorship.

44520.q: Under Art. 36 of the Federal Constitution, what legal basis is enough for a minor restriction of a fundamental right?
44520.e: Minor restrictions may be based on a law in the material sense, which includes an ordinance of the government. Only serious restrictions need an act passed by parliament.
44520.m: An ordinance is enough for minor restrictions of fundamental rights.

44521.q: Under Art. 36 of the Federal Constitution, what basis does a serious restriction of a fundamental right need?
a: A law in the formal sense
44521.e: Serious restrictions must be laid down in the act itself, which was passed by parliament and is subject to referendum.
44521.m: The more serious a restriction of fundamental rights, the more clearly a law must regulate it.

44522.q: In which case does Art. 36 of the Federal Constitution allow a restriction of fundamental rights without a legal basis?
a: In case of serious, immediate danger that cannot be averted otherwise
With a majority in the municipal council
44522.e: This exception is called the general police clause. It only applies to real emergencies that lawmakers could not foresee.
44522.m: Only in real emergencies may the state restrict fundamental rights without a law.

44523.q: Which court in Switzerland decides as the highest authority whether cantonal authorities have violated a fundamental right?
a: The High Court of the Canton of Bern
44523.e: The Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne is the highest court in Switzerland. Anyone who feels their fundamental rights have been violated can take the case all the way there.
44523.m: The Federal Supreme Court has the final say on violations of fundamental rights.

44524.q: Besides the public interest, what is an allowed reason for restricting a fundamental right?
a: Protecting the fundamental rights of others
44524.e: The fundamental rights of different people can clash, for example freedom of expression and protection of personality. Then one may be restricted in favour of the other.
44524.m: Fundamental rights can be restricted to protect the rights of others.

44525.q: What does Art. 36 para. 4 of the Federal Constitution lay down to protect fundamental rights?
a: The essence of fundamental rights is inviolable.
Fundamental rights apply only to Swiss citizens.
Emergency law may cancel all fundamental rights.
Fundamental rights bind only the cantons.
44525.e: Even if the other conditions of Art. 36 are met, a restriction may never touch the essence of a fundamental right. This innermost core is beyond any weighing up.
44525.m: The state may never violate the essence of a fundamental right.

44526.q: What does a court examine under the heading “public interest” when a fundamental right is restricted?
a: Whether the restriction serves a legitimate aim of the community
Whether the majority likes the restriction
Whether the restriction brings in money
44526.e: Allowed aims include, for example, public safety, health, environmental protection or peace and order. Purely financial interests are usually not enough.
44526.m: Restricting a fundamental right needs a legitimate aim in the interest of the community.

44527.q: Which restriction of fundamental rights during the Covid-19 pandemic was based, among other things, on the Epidemics Act?
a: Abolition of the right to vote
44527.e: The Confederation and the cantons restricted freedom of assembly and economic freedom, based on the Epidemics Act and emergency ordinances.
44527.m: Even in the pandemic, restrictions of fundamental rights needed a legal basis.

44528.q: Which three parts does the principle of proportionality include?
44528.e: A measure must be able to achieve its aim, be the mildest effective means and stand in reasonable relation to the restriction.
44528.m: A measure is only proportionate if it is suitable, necessary and reasonable.

44529.q: Where in Switzerland is it laid down that all state action must be proportionate?
44529.e: Art. 5 para. 2 of the Federal Constitution requires state action to be in the public interest and proportionate.
44529.m: All state action must be proportionate.

44530.q: What does the necessity test examine?
a: Whether there is no milder, equally effective means
Whether the measure has been used before
44530.e: If there is a means that achieves the aim just as well with less interference, the stricter measure is not necessary.
44530.m: The state must choose the mildest effective means.

44531.q: Which saying describes a breach of the principle of proportionality?
a: To use a sledgehammer to crack a nut
To set the fox to guard the henhouse
To buy a pig in a poke
To not see the wood for the trees
